paraphrase: Because one is struck by the three kinds of suffering, there arises the desire to know the means of striking them down. If it is objected that the inquiry is pointless because visible means exist, (the answer is) no, because those means do not remove suffering with certainty or finally.

original.text: duḥkhatrayābhighātāj jijñāsā tadabhighātake hetau / dṛṣṭe sāpārthā cen naikāntātyantato 'bhāvāt

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: The verse says only 'the three sufferings'; the names ādhyātmika, ādhibhautika, ādhidaivika are supplied by the commentaries (Gauḍapāda, Māṭhara, Vācaspati). Variant: tad-apaghātake / tad-avaghātake.

paraphrase: The means known from Vedic tradition (ānuśravika) are like the visible means, for they are bound up with impurity, decay and gradation. The opposite means is better: the discriminating knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower.

original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Commentators explain the impurity (aviśuddhi) as arising from the killing of animals in sacrifice (Gauḍapāda, Vācaspati). Māṭhara reads 'aviśuddhaḥ kṣayātiśayayuktaḥ'.

paraphrase: Root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; the seven beginning with the great one (mahat) are both producers and modifications; the group of sixteen is modification only; puruṣa is neither producer nor modification.

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Three means of valid knowledge are accepted — perception, inference and reliable testimony — since every other means is established within these; for what is to be known is established through a means of knowledge.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Perception is the determination (adhyavasāya) concerning each (sense-)object; inference is declared to be threefold and preceded by (knowledge of) the mark and what bears the mark; reliable testimony is reliable revelation (āptaśruti).
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: The three kinds of inference are named by the commentators (pūrvavat, śeṣavat, sāmānyatodṛṣṭa); Vācaspati also divides inference into vīta and avīta.

paraphrase: Things beyond the senses are known through inference from general correlation (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa); what is imperceptible and not established even by that is established by reliable scripture.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Variants: prasiddhir for pratītir; sādhyam for siddham.

paraphrase: (Existing things are not perceived) because of excessive distance, excessive nearness, impairment of the senses, inattention of the mind, subtlety, obstruction, being overpowered, and mixture with what is similar.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Its (prakṛti's) non-perception is due to subtlety, not to non-existence; it is apprehended through its effects. That effect is the great one (mahat) and the rest, unlike prakṛti and also like it.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The effect exists (in its cause before production): because the non-existent cannot be produced; because a definite material cause is taken up; because not everything arises from everything; because a capable cause produces only what it is capable of producing; and because the effect has the nature of its cause.

original.text: asadakaraṇād upādānagrahaṇāt sarvasaṃbhavābhāvāt / śaktasya śakyakaraṇāt kāraṇabhāvāc ca satkāryam
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The manifest has a cause, is impermanent, non-pervasive, active, many, dependent (on its cause), a mark (that merges back), composed of parts and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The manifest consists of the three guṇas, is non-discriminating, an object, common, unconscious and productive; so too is pradhāna. Puruṣa is the opposite of these, and also (in other respects) similar.

original.text: triguṇam aviveki viṣayaḥ sāmānyam acetanaṃ prasavadharmi / vyaktaṃ tathā pradhānaṃ tadviparītas tathā ca pumān
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Commentators explain puruṣa's similarity as sharing with the unmanifest the properties of being uncaused, eternal, pervasive etc. (cf. SK 10).

paraphrase: The guṇas have the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion; they serve to illuminate, to activate and to restrain; and they function by dominating, supporting and producing one another and by being paired together.

original.text: prītyaprītiviṣādātmakāḥ prakāśapravṛttiniyamārthāḥ / anyonyābhibhavāśrayajananamithunavṛttayaś ca guṇāḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas stimulating and mobile; tamas heavy and enveloping. Their functioning (together) serves a purpose, like a lamp.

original.text: sattvaṃ laghu prakāśakam iṣṭam upaṣṭambhakaṃ calaṃ ca rajaḥ / guru varaṇakam eva tamaḥ pradīpavac cārthato vṛttiḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Commentators explain the lamp: oil, wick and flame, though opposed, together give light.

paraphrase: Non-discrimination and the other properties (of the manifest) are established because it consists of the three guṇas and their opposite is absent (in it); the unmanifest too is established, because an effect has the nature of the guṇas of its cause.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: The first half has several variant readings (see Ruzsa's apparatus).

paraphrase: (The unmanifest exists as cause) because particular things are limited in measure; because of their homogeneity; because activity proceeds from a potency; because cause and effect are distinguished; and because the whole manifold world merges back (into non-distinction).
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The unmanifest exists as cause. It operates through the three guṇas, by their combination and by transformation, like water, (becoming different) according to the differences of the abodes of the respective guṇas.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Water is the commentators' image of rain, one in taste, becoming different in different receptacles.

paraphrase: Puruṣa exists: because aggregates are for the sake of another; because there must be something opposite to what has the three guṇas and the rest; because there must be a controller; because there is an enjoyer; and because activity is for the sake of isolation.

original.text: saṃghātaparārthatvāt triguṇādiviparyayād adhiṣṭhānāt / puruṣo 'sti bhoktṛbhāvāt kaivalyārthaṃ pravṛtteś ca
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The plurality of puruṣas is established: because birth, death and the instruments are allotted to each separately; because (beings) do not act all at once; and because of differences in the (proportion of the) three guṇas.

original.text: jananamaraṇakaraṇānāṃ pratiniyamād ayugapatpravṛtteś ca / puruṣabahutvaṃ siddhaṃ traiguṇyaviparyayāc caiva
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Variant: janma- for janana-.

paraphrase: And from that contrast (with the guṇas) it is established that this puruṣa is witness, isolated, neutral, seer and non-agent.

original.text: tasmāc ca viparyāsāt siddhaṃ sākṣitvam asya puruṣasya / kaivalyaṃ mādhyasthyaṃ draṣṭṛtvam akartṛbhāvaś ca
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Therefore, from conjunction with it (puruṣa), the unconscious subtle body (liṅga) appears as if conscious; and though agency belongs to the guṇas, the indifferent one (puruṣa) appears as if the agent.

original.text: tasmāt tatsaṃyogād acetanaṃ cetanāvad iva liṅgam / guṇakartṛtve ca tathā karteva bhavaty udāsīnaḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The conjunction of the two — for the sake of seeing (named with puruṣa) and for the sake of isolation (named with pradhāna) — is like that of the lame man and the blind man; creation is produced by it.

original.text: puruṣasya darśanārthaṃ kaivalyārthaṃ tathā pradhānasya / paṅgvandhavad ubhayor api saṃyogas tatkṛtaḥ sargaḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Commentators construe the genitives differently (e.g., Vācaspati: for pradhāna to be seen by puruṣa, and for puruṣa's isolation).

paraphrase: From prakṛti (arises) the great one (mahat); from that, the I-maker (ahaṃkāra); from that, the group of sixteen; and from five among those sixteen, the five gross elements.

original.text: prakṛter mahāṃs tato 'haṃkāras tasmād gaṇaś ca ṣoḍaśakaḥ / tasmād api ṣoḍaśakāt pañcabhyaḥ pañca bhūtāni
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Buddhi is determination (adhyavasāya). Virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power are its sāttvika form; its tāmasa form is the reverse of these.

original.text: adhyavasāyo buddhir dharmo jñānaṃ virāga aiśvaryam / sāttvikam etad rūpaṃ tāmasam asmād viparyastam
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Ahaṃkāra is self-assertion (abhimāna). From it a twofold creation proceeds: the group of eleven (organs) and the group of five subtle elements.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The sāttvika group of eleven proceeds from ahaṃkāra as modified (vaikṛta); the subtle elements from (ahaṃkāra as) bhūtādi, which is tāmasa; both (groups) from (ahaṃkāra as) taijasa.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The sense capacities (buddhīndriya) are named ear, skin, eye, tongue and nose; speech, hands, feet, anus and genitals are called the capacities of action (karmendriya).
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: The order of the sense capacities differs between recensions.

paraphrase: Here mind (manas) partakes of both (kinds); it constructs (saṅkalpaka) and is a capacity (indriya) by similarity (with the others). The diversity (of the organs) comes from particular transformations of the guṇas and from the differences of external objects.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: V2 and the Yuktidīpikā read a different verse here (mind as instrument of both kinds, internal, of the three times).

paraphrase: The function of the five (sense capacities) with regard to sound and the rest is mere awareness (ālocana); speaking, grasping, walking, excreting and delight are (the functions) of the (other) five.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Variant: rūpādiṣu for śabdādiṣu.

paraphrase: The (three internal organs) each have their own characteristic function, which is not shared; the shared function of the instruments is the five vital winds, prāṇa and the rest.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: With regard to what is perceived, the functioning of the four (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas and a sense) is taught to be simultaneous and also successive; with regard to what is not perceived, the functioning of the three is preceded by that.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The instruments take up their own functions prompted by one another's impulse; puruṣa's purpose alone is the cause; the instrument is not made to act by anyone.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The instrument is of thirteen kinds; it seizes, holds and illuminates; its object is tenfold — what is to be seized, held and illuminated.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The internal instrument is threefold, the external tenfold, called the objects (i.e., presenting objects) of the three. The external operates in present time; the internal instrument in all three times.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Of these, the five sense capacities have specific and non-specific objects; speech has sound as its object; the rest (of the action capacities) have all five objects.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Since buddhi together with the internal organs apprehends every object, the threefold instrument is the door-keeper and the rest are the doors.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: These (organs), particular modifications of the guṇas, differing from one another, illuminate like lamps the whole purpose of puruṣa and present it to buddhi.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Because buddhi accomplishes every experience of puruṣa, it is also buddhi that discriminates the subtle difference between pradhāna and puruṣa.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The subtle elements are non-specific; from these five come the five gross elements; these are called specific, and they are calm, turbulent and dull.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Subtle (bodies), (bodies) born of mother and father, and the gross elements: these are the three kinds of specifics. Of these the subtle are constant; those born of mother and father perish.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The subtle body (liṅga) — produced first, unattached, constant, (made of the principles) from mahat down to the subtle elements — transmigrates, without enjoyment (of its own), perfumed by the dispositions (bhāva).

original.text: pūrvotpannam asaktaṃ niyataṃ mahadādisūkṣmaparyantam / saṃsarati nirupabhogaṃ bhāvair adhivāsitaṃ liṅgam
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: As a picture does not stand without a support, or a shadow without a post and the like, so the subtle body does not subsist without a support, without the specifics.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Some editions read 'without the non-specifics' (vinā 'viśeṣaiḥ).

paraphrase: Motivated by the purpose of puruṣa, this subtle body, through the connection of occasioning causes and their results and through the pervasive power of prakṛti, plays its parts like an actor.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The dispositions — virtue and the rest — are seen to be innate, natural and acquired; they rest on the instrument (buddhi), while the embryonic stages beginning with the kalala rest on the effect (the body).
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Through virtue there is upward movement, through non-virtue downward movement; through knowledge, liberation; through the reverse, bondage is held to follow.

original.text: dharmeṇa gamanam ūrdhvaṃ gamanam adhastād bhavaty adharmeṇa / jñānena cāpavargo viparyayād iṣyate bandhaḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Through dispassion, absorption into prakṛti; through passion of the nature of rajas, saṃsāra; through power, non-obstruction; through their reverse, the reverse.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Commentators explain: dispassion without knowledge of the principles leads to absorption in prakṛti, not to liberation.

paraphrase: This is the creation of cognitions (pratyaya-sarga), called error, incapacity, contentment and accomplishment; through the suppression (of one guṇa by another) due to the inequality of the guṇas, its divisions are fifty.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: There are five kinds of error; of incapacity, due to defects of the instruments, twenty-eight kinds; contentment is ninefold, accomplishment eightfold.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Darkness (tamas) has eight divisions, and so has delusion (moha); great delusion is tenfold; gloom (tāmisra) is eighteenfold, and so is blind gloom (andhatāmisra).
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Incapacity is declared to be the injuries of the eleven organs together with the injuries of buddhi; the injuries of buddhi are seventeen, through the reversal of the contentments and accomplishments.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Nine contentments are declared: four internal, called nature, means, time and fortune; and five external, arising from abstention from (the five) objects.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Variant: abhimatāḥ / abhihitāḥ.

paraphrase: Reasoning, (hearing) words, study, the three destructions of suffering, gaining friends, and giving are the eight accomplishments; the preceding three (error, incapacity, contentment) are the threefold curb of accomplishment.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Without the dispositions there is no subtle body; without the subtle body the dispositions do not come about; hence creation is twofold, called that of the liṅga and that of the dispositions.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The divine (creation) is of eight kinds, the animal of five, and the human of one kind; this in brief is the creation of beings.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Above, (creation) abounds in sattva; at the root, in tamas; in the middle, in rajas — from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: There the conscious puruṣa undergoes suffering produced by old age and death, until the subtle body ceases; hence suffering is by nature.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Variant ending samāsena ('in brief') for svabhāvena ('by nature').

paraphrase: Thus this undertaking of prakṛti, from mahat down to the specific elements, is for the liberation of each puruṣa — for another's sake, as if for its own.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: The Yuktidīpikā reads a different first half (pravartate tattvabhūtabhāvākhyaḥ).

paraphrase: As unconscious milk flows for the growth of the calf, so pradhāna acts for the liberation of puruṣa.

original.text: vatsavivṛddhinimittaṃ kṣīrasya yathā pravṛttir ajñasya / puruṣavimokṣanimittaṃ tathā pravṛttiḥ pradhānasya
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: As people engage in actions to satisfy a longing, so the unmanifest acts for the liberation of puruṣa.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: As a dancer, having shown herself to the audience, ceases from dancing, so prakṛti, having shown herself to puruṣa, ceases.

original.text: raṅgasya darśayitvā nivartate nartakī yathā nṛtyāt / puruṣasya tathātmānaṃ prakāśya vinivartate prakṛtiḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: By manifold means prakṛti — helpful, possessed of the guṇas — acts purposelessly (for herself) for the sake of puruṣa, who does not help (her) and is without guṇas.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Nothing, I think, is more modest than prakṛti, who, (knowing) 'I have been seen', does not come into puruṣa's sight again.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Gauḍapāda uses this verse to argue that neither Īśvara, nature nor time, but prakṛti, is the cause.

paraphrase: Therefore no one (no puruṣa) is in truth bound, released, or transmigrates; it is prakṛti, in its various abodes, that transmigrates, is bound and is released.

original.text: tasmān na badhyate 'ddhā na mucyate nāpi saṃsarati kaścit / saṃsarati badhyate mucyate ca nānāśrayā prakṛtiḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Māṭhara reads 'nāpi mucyate' for ''ddhā na mucyate'.

paraphrase: The three sufferings are: internal (ādhyātmika), bodily — from imbalance of wind, bile and phlegm, like fever and dysentery — and mental — from separation from the dear and union with the undesired; from other beings (ādhibhautika), from humans, animals, birds, reptiles, insects and plants, born of womb, egg, sweat or sprout; and from the divine (ādhidaivika), such as cold, heat, wind, rain and lightning. Medicine and protection are seen remedies, but they do not remove suffering with certainty or permanently.
speaker: Gauḍapāda

paraphrase: The Vedic means (ānuśravika) are like the seen means: the Veda promises immortality through soma ('we have drunk soma, we have become immortal') and that one who performs the horse sacrifice crosses death and sin, but these means are impure through the killing of animals, perishable, and graded; the better means is the knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower.
speaker: Gauḍapāda

paraphrase: Synonyms: prakṛti is called pradhāna, brahman, the unmanifest, bahudhānaka and māyā; mahat is called buddhi, āsurī, mati, khyāti, jñāna and prajñā; ahaṃkāra is called bhūtādi, vaikṛta, taijasa and abhimāna. From the subtle elements of sound, touch, form, taste and smell arise space, air, fire, water and earth respectively.
speaker: Gauḍapāda

paraphrase: Dharma is marked by compassion, giving and the restraints and observances taught in the Pātañjala (non-harming, truth, non-stealing, continence, non-possession; purity, contentment, austerity, study, devotion to Īśvara). Knowledge is external — the Vedas with their six limbs, Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra — leading only to worldly esteem, or internal — knowledge of prakṛti and puruṣa — leading to liberation. Dispassion is external — aversion to seen objects from seeing the faults of acquiring, guarding, loss, attachment and harm — or internal, seeing even pradhāna as like a dream or magic show. Power is eightfold: becoming minute, great, light, reaching, irresistible will, lordship, control, and going wherever one wishes.
speaker: Gauḍapāda
notes: Gauḍapāda's list of powers names nine terms (incl. garimā) while calling it eightfold.

paraphrase: The dispositions are innate (sāṃsiddhika), as the four born with Kapila at the first creation; natural (prākṛta), as in Brahmā's four sons Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana and Sanatkumāra at sixteen; and acquired (vaikṛta), as in us, where knowledge arises with the teacher's form as its occasioning cause, from knowledge dispassion, from dispassion virtue, from virtue power.
speaker: Gauḍapāda

paraphrase: The sixty-two forms of error: darkness (eightfold) is dissolving into the eight prakṛtis (pradhāna, buddhi, ahaṃkāra, the five subtle elements) and thinking 'I am liberated'; delusion (eightfold) is attachment to the eight powers, through which gods like Indra fail to reach liberation and fall back; great delusion (tenfold) is attachment to the five objects, divine and human; gloom (eighteenfold) is taking delight in the prosperity of the eight powers and ten objects and not accepting their loss; blind gloom (eighteenfold) is the great suffering of one who dies amid enjoyment or falls from the powers.
speaker: Gauḍapāda

paraphrase: The contentments: 'nature' — knowing prakṛti and resting content, without liberation; 'means' — taking up the triple staff, water-pot and the like, thinking liberation comes from them, without knowing the principles; 'time' — thinking liberation will come in time, so why practise the principles; 'fortune' — thinking it will come by luck; and five external ones from turning away from the five objects on seeing the faults of acquiring, guarding, loss, attachment and harm. Their names in another treatise are ambhas, salila, ogha, vṛṣṭi, sutamas, pāra, sunetra, nārīka and anuttamāmbhasika.
speaker: Gauḍapāda

paraphrase: The accomplishments: reasoning (one who constantly reflects 'what is true, what is highest, what is the final good' comes to know that puruṣa is other than pradhāna); words (knowledge from hearing); study (of the Vedas and other texts, gaining knowledge of the twenty-five principles); the three destructions of suffering (approaching a teacher for instruction to destroy the three sufferings); gaining a friend who has knowledge; and giving (serving the venerable with shelter, medicine, staff, water-pot, food and clothing, and receiving knowledge from them). Error, incapacity and contentment are a goad that holds the world in ignorance like an elephant; abandoning them, one should resort to accomplishment, from which knowledge of the principles and liberation follow.
speaker: Gauḍapāda
notes: Other-treatise names given: tāra, sutāra, tāratāra, pramoda, pramudita, pramodamāna, ramyaka, sadāpramudita.

paraphrase: Some say Īśvara is the cause ('this unknowing creature, not master of its own pleasure and pain, goes to heaven or hell impelled by Īśvara'); others say nature (svabhāva) ('who whitened the swans, who painted the peacocks?'), or time. The Sāṃkhya teachers reply: how could beings with guṇas be born from Īśvara, who is without guṇas, or from puruṣa, also without guṇas? As white cloth comes from white threads, the three worlds with the three guṇas come from pradhāna with the three guṇas. Time is included in the manifest, nature merges into it; so prakṛti alone is the cause.
speaker: Gauḍapāda

paraphrase: Prakṛti is one only, the principal cause of the three worlds; there is no second prakṛti. Though prakṛti and puruṣa, both all-pervading, remain conjoined, there is no purpose for creation, since both purposes — experience of objects and apprehension of the difference between the guṇas and puruṣa — are fulfilled.
speaker: Gauḍapāda

paraphrase: Though perfect knowledge of the twenty-five principles has arisen, the yogin remains bearing a body through the force of impressions, as a potter's wheel keeps turning after the pot is made. The seven binding forms, burnt by right knowledge like seeds burnt by fire, can no longer sprout; knowledge burns future karma, present karma is exhausted, and with the exhaustion of impressions liberation comes at the fall of the body.
speaker: Gauḍapāda

paraphrase: The supreme sage is the blessed sage Kapila; the knowledge is secret; through considering the persistence, manifestation and disappearance of beings arises the understanding that discriminates the twenty-five principles. A closing verse says the Sāṃkhya taught by the sage Kapila is the cause of release from saṃsāra, set out in these seventy āryās, with a bhāṣya made by Gauḍapāda.
speaker: Gauḍapāda

paraphrase: The blessed great sage Kapila, endowed with innate virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power, an avatāra of the ancient Person, was born to Prajāpati Kardama and Devahūti, daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu. Moved by compassion for the world in blind darkness, he found the brahmin of the Āsuri clan, who had sacrificed for a thousand years, and asked 'Āsuri, do you delight in the householder's life?' — 'I do.' He returned after another thousand years and again after a third; then Āsuri answered 'I do not delight', and, struck by the three sufferings, gave up house, wife and children and became Kapila's disciple.
speaker: Māṭhara

paraphrase: The knowledge is a purifier because it saves from falling into hells, ghost-realms and animal births, and foremost — above Veda, Purāṇa, Bhārata and the law-books — because it removes suffering certainly and finally. Kapila gave it to Āsuri, having recognized his fitness, out of compassion, as a friend who helps all without expecting return; Āsuri gave it to Pañcaśikha, who divided the doctrine and gave it to many pupils.
speaker: Māṭhara

paraphrase: The knowledge came from Kapila to Āsuri, then to Pañcaśikha, from him to Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others, and from them to Īśvarakṛṣṇa, who, afraid of lengthy books, condensed the Ṣaṣṭitantra in āryā verses. The Ṣaṣṭitantra is the treatise in which sixty topics are set out.
speaker: Māṭhara

paraphrase: The sixty topics are the fifty cognitions (five errors, twenty-eight incapacities, nine contentments, eight accomplishments) and ten fundamental ones: existence (of pradhāna), its oneness, its purposiveness, (puruṣa's) otherness, (prakṛti's) being for another, cessation, conjunction, separation, the plurality of puruṣas, and the persistence of the body (after knowledge).
speaker: Māṭhara

paraphrase: The sage told the great doctrine to the brahmin Āsuri, who sought the truth, for the removal of the three sufferings; since it could not be mastered even in hundreds of years, wise sages condensed it; rival teachers built intricate arguments in their own treatises; therefore Īśvarakṛṣṇa made this concise work called the Seventy, which is nevertheless a complete treatise.

The opponents of the doctrine are those who hold puruṣa, Īśvara or atoms (as the cause), the destructionists (vaināśika), the prākṛtikas and those who take a modification to be the self; the teachers built difficult arguments to defeat them.

The ten fundamental topics are: the existence of pradhāna, its oneness, its purposiveness, (puruṣa's) distinctness, being for another, the plurality (of puruṣas), separation, conjunction, the remaining function, and non-agency; with the fivefold error, the ninefold contentment, the twenty-eightfold incapacity of the instruments and the eight accomplishments, these make sixty topics.

The teachers disagree on emergence: some place an indescribable principle between pradhāna and mahat; for Patañjali, Pañcādhikaraṇa and Vārṣagaṇa mahat arises from pradhāna; for Vindhyavāsin six non-specifics (ahaṃkāra and the five subtle elements) arise from mahat. All derive the organs from ahaṃkāra, but Pañcādhikaraṇa holds them elemental; Vārṣagaṇya holds the subtle elements cumulative; Vindhyavāsin holds the organs all-pervading, the instrument elevenfold, apprehension in manas, and the functions of saṅkalpa, abhimāna and adhyavasāya one.

On transmigration the teachers disagree: for Pañcādhikaraṇa a conveying (ātivāhika) subtle body, permanent, enters semen and blood at conception and is clothed and unclothed by the perishable outer body; for Patañjali a subtle body leads the organs to the womb and ceases, another arising at death; for Vindhyavāsin, since the organs are all-pervading, birth is their functioning at the seed-place and death its abandonment, so there is no subtle body.

The dispositions are innate, natural or acquired. Innate: the supreme sage's knowledge, arising with his body like light with a lamp; likewise the virtue of Bhṛgu and others and the dispassion of Sanaka and others. Natural: Āsuri's dispassion, arising from contact with the supreme sage; Nandin's power from contact with Maheśvara; Nahuṣa's virtue from contact with Agastya. Acquired: ours. Against Vindhyavāsin, who held even the sage's knowledge to be acquired, and Pañcādhikaraṇa, who derived all from another.

Objection: the Sāṃkhya teacher Paurika holds that each puruṣa has its own pradhāna producing its body, and that when the pradhāna of the great-bodied one operates the others operate, and when it ceases they cease. Reply: one prakṛti is accepted, because there is no means of knowledge for many — they are beyond the senses and there is no unambiguous inferential mark.

The supreme sage gave the teaching not for merit, wealth or pleasure, nor for his own liberation, which his innate knowledge secured, but out of compassion, seeing Āsuri afflicted by the three sufferings and wishing that, as for himself, suffering should cease for Āsuri and through him for others. Because the doctrine began with the Blessed One, its lineage cannot be recounted even in hundreds of thousands of years.

The doctrine came through Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others; since the older works had grown too long for people of short life, Īśvarakṛṣṇa, out of compassion, gathered the statements of the Ṣaṣṭitantra, separated from their tales, into seventy verses.
notes: The e-text has a lacuna just before the list.

paraphrase: Because Nārāyaṇa, Manu, Janaka, Vasiṣṭha, Dvaipāyana and other teachers accepted, taught and praised pradhāna, puruṣa and the other categories, Īśvarakṛṣṇa examined them by reasoning, following the scripture of the supreme sage and giving precedence to the three means of knowledge.

The purpose of the treatise is liberation through knowledge of the principles, which are twenty-five: 'the knower of the twenty-five principles, delighting in whatever stage of life, with matted hair, shaven head or tuft, is liberated, no doubt'. Because the Ṣaṣṭitantra is extensive, the Seventy was begun for those who like brevity. Liberation brings the cessation of suffering; the one who does not know the principles, struck by sufferings, keeps transmigrating.

What is said in the Seventy covers the topics of the entire Ṣaṣṭitantra, but without tales and without the objections of opponents — pure topics useful for bondage and liberation; hence the Seventy is complete.

Suffering is threefold: internal — bodily, from imbalance of wind, bile and phlegm, and mental, from desire, anger, greed, delusion, fear, envy and not seeing particular objects — curable by internal means; from other beings, caused by humans, beasts, birds, reptiles and plants; and from the divine, caused by possession by yakṣas, rākṣasas, vināyakas, planets and the like — both curable by external means. Suffering is a modification of rajas felt by each; its contact with the conscious power as something disagreeable is the 'striking'. Seen remedies — medicine, pleasures, statecraft, gems and spells — fail to remove it certainly and finally.
speaker: Vācaspati Miśra

paraphrase: The better means is the direct realization of the distinctness of sattva (buddhi) and puruṣa: having heard the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower discriminatingly from śruti, smṛti, itihāsa and purāṇa, and established them by the reasoning of the treatise, one cultivates the principles through long, reverent, uninterrupted meditative practice, from which arises the knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I', complete, pure and single.
speaker: Vācaspati Miśra

paraphrase: The impurity of the Vedic means is that soma and other sacrifices involve killing animals and seeds; as the teacher Pañcaśikha says, 'a slight admixture, removable, bearable': the demerit from the killing is small, can be removed by expiation, and if not, is borne amid the ocean of merit's delights. The general prohibition 'do not harm any being' is not cancelled by the specific injunction to offer the animal to Agni-Soma, because they have different objects: the prohibition makes known that harming causes evil to the agent, the injunction that it serves the sacrifice.
speaker: Vācaspati Miśra

paraphrase: Perception is buddhi's determination — a predominance of sattva over tamas — when a sense is in contact with its object. Buddhi, being of prakṛti, is unconscious; puruṣa, reflected in it and taking on its shade, appears to have knowledge and pleasure, while buddhi, taking on the shade of consciousness, appears conscious. Inference is vīta (affirmative) or avīta (by exclusion; = śeṣavat), and vīta is pūrvavat or sāmānyatodṛṣṭa. Testimony from the authorless Veda is self-valid, and Kapila at the start of the eon could remember the Veda learned in a prior eon.
speaker: Vācaspati Miśra

paraphrase: Postulation (arthāpatti) is a form of inference; absence (abhāva) is perception of a particular transformation of the ground; inclusion (sambhava) is inference; tradition without a named speaker (aitihya) is not a means of knowledge unless the speaker is reliable, when it is testimony. Hence three means of knowledge.
speaker: Vācaspati Miśra

paraphrase: Of the eight accomplishments the three destructions of suffering are primary and the other five are means to them in order: study of the texts from a teacher, understanding their meaning (śabda), examination by reasoning (ūha), confirmation with teachers and fellow students (suhṛtprāpti), and 'dāna' as the purification of discriminative knowledge (from the root 'dai', to purify).
speaker: Vācaspati Miśra
notes: From memory; the local DCS text covers only SK 1–15. Verify order and etymology.

paraphrase: Vācaspati quotes the Rājavārttika listing the sixty topics: pradhāna's existence, oneness, purposiveness, distinctness, being for another, plurality (of puruṣas), separation, conjunction, the remaining function and non-agency — ten fundamental topics — with five errors, nine contentments, twenty-eight incapacities and eight accomplishments.
speaker: Vācaspati Miśra

paraphrase: Now, the complete cessation of the threefold suffering is the supreme human goal.

paraphrase: The ten fundamental topics — existence (of pradhāna and puruṣa), oneness, purposiveness, being for another, otherness, non-agency, conjunction, separation, the plurality of puruṣas and the persistence of the body — are each proved by a Kārikā verse; with the fifty cognitions they are the sixty topics called Ṣaṣṭitantra.

paraphrase: Bondage is threefold: bondage to prakṛti (absorption in prakṛti by taking the eight prakṛtis as highest); bondage to the modifications (of renunciants and worldly people ruled by the senses and attached to objects); and bondage through gifts (of students, householders, mendicants and forest-dwellers who give gifts with self-conceit, their minds struck by desire and delusion).
